x:
The octopus may be one of the cleverest creatures in the ocean. It has eight flexible arms lined with suckers, and each sucker can taste as well as grip. An octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak. Scientists have watched octopuses open jars, solve simple puzzles, and even escape from their tanks at night.

Octopuses are also masters of disguise. Special cells in their skin let them change color in less than a second, and some can change the texture of their skin to look like rocks or coral. If a predator gets too close, an octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink and jet away. Surprisingly, an octopus has three hearts and blue blood. Most kinds live for only a year or two, but they pack a lot of learning into that short time.

Every fall, millions of monarch butterflies in the eastern United States and Canada begin an incredible journey. They fly south, sometimes traveling more than 2,000 miles, to reach the mountain forests of central Mexico. There, they cluster together on fir trees by the thousands, covering the branches like orange leaves. The cool mountain air helps them rest through the winter without using too much energy.

What makes this trip so amazing is that no single butterfly has made it before. The monarchs that fly south are the great-grandchildren, or even great-great-grandchildren, of the ones that left Mexico the spring before. In March, they head north again, laying eggs on milkweed plants along the way. Scientists are still studying how monarchs find their way, but they think the butterflies use the position of the Sun as a guide.

Saturday, April 12

This morning, I set up the bird feeder that Grandpa and I built from scrap wood. I filled it with sunflower seeds and hung it from the maple tree outside the kitchen window. For almost an hour, nothing happened, and I began to think my plan had failed. Then a pair of chickadees appeared, followed by a bright red cardinal.

By lunchtime, I had counted seven different species. The blue jays were the loudest, and they chased the smaller birds away whenever they arrived. A downy woodpecker clung to the side of the feeder instead of perching on it. I sketched each bird in my notebook and wrote down the time I saw it. Tomorrow, I'm going to add a dish of water, because Grandpa says birds need a place to drink and bathe, too.

Camels are perfectly suited to life in the desert, where water is scarce and temperatures can swing from scorching days to chilly nights. Many people believe that a camel's hump stores water, but that isn't true. The hump is actually made of fat, which the camel's body can break down for energy when food is hard to find.

A camel can go for days without drinking, and when it finally reaches water, it can gulp down more than 25 gallons in just a few minutes. Its long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep out blowing sand, while its wide, padded feet keep it from sinking into the dunes. For thousands of years, people in Africa and Asia have relied on camels to carry goods across vast deserts, so camels are sometimes called ships of the desert.

Have you ever rubbed a balloon on your hair and watched it stick to a wall? Have you felt a tiny shock when you touched a doorknob after walking across a carpet? Both of these surprises are caused by static electricity.

Everything around us is made of atoms, and atoms contain tiny particles called electrons. When two materials rub together, some electrons can jump from one to the other. The object that gains extra electrons becomes negatively charged, while the one that loses them becomes positively charged. Opposite charges attract each other, so the balloon clings to the wall. When you touch a doorknob, the extra charge rushes away all at once, and you feel a spark. Static shocks happen more often in winter, because dry air lets charges build up more easily than damp air does.

For the science fair, Elena and I decided to test which of three kinds of paper towels soaked up the most water. We called them Towel A, Towel B, and Towel C so that we wouldn't be influenced by the packages. First, we cut each towel into a square of the same size. Then we dipped each square into a cup of water for ten seconds and let it drip for another ten.

After that, we squeezed each towel into an empty measuring cup and recorded how much water came out. We repeated the test five times for each towel, because one trial is never enough to trust. Towel B held the most water every single time, even though it was the cheapest. Our teacher, Mr. Okafor, said our best decision was keeping everything the same except the towel. Scientists call that a fair test.

In summer, most leaves are green because they are full of chlorophyll, a substance that helps plants turn sunlight, water, and air into food. Chlorophyll is so plentiful that it hides the other colors in the leaf. Yellow and orange pigments are there all summer long, but we simply can't see them.

As autumn arrives, the days grow shorter and the nights become cooler. Trees such as maples, oaks, and birches respond by slowly shutting down their food-making factories. The chlorophyll breaks down, and the hidden yellows and oranges finally appear. Some trees also make new red and purple pigments in the fall, especially when the days are sunny and the nights are crisp. Eventually, the leaves drop to the ground, and the trees rest until spring. Then they grow fresh green leaves, and the cycle begins again.

Germs are living things so small that you need a microscope to see them. Many are harmless, and some even help us digest food. However, certain germs can make people sick, and they spread easily from hands to faces, doorknobs, and shared pencils.

In the 1840s, a Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that fewer patients got sick when doctors washed their hands. At the time, many people didn't believe him, but later scientists proved he was right. Today, washing your hands is one of the best ways to stay healthy. Wet your hands, add soap, and scrub for at least twenty seconds, which is about as long as singing the birthday song twice. Don't forget the backs of your hands, between your fingers, and under your nails. Then rinse them well and dry them with a clean towel.

Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun, and its rings make it one of the most beautiful sights in the solar system. From far away, the rings look solid, but they are actually made of countless pieces of ice and rock. Some are as tiny as grains of sand, while others are as large as houses. The rings stretch out for many thousands of miles, yet in most places they are surprisingly thin.

Galileo was the first person to see Saturn's rings through a telescope, in 1610, but his telescope was too weak to show them clearly. He thought the planet had two large moons on either side! Decades later, astronomers realized that the strange bulges were rings. Saturn is not the only planet with rings, though. Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune have them too, but theirs are much fainter.

t: One Small Step on the Moon
x:
On July 20, 1969, millions of people around the world gathered around their televisions. They were watching the Apollo 11 mission, which had carried three astronauts to the Moon. While Michael Collins circled overhead in the command module, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the surface in a small craft called the Eagle.

Armstrong climbed down the ladder first. As he stepped onto the dusty ground, he said, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." Aldrin soon joined him, and the two men collected rocks, took photographs, and set up experiments. Their footprints are probably still there today, because the Moon has no wind or rain to wash them away. The astronauts returned safely to Earth four days later, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean.

Comets are sometimes called dirty snowballs, because they are made of ice, dust, and rock. Most of the time, they travel in the cold, distant parts of the solar system, far beyond Neptune. Every so often, however, a comet's long, oval path brings it close to the Sun. As it warms up, some of its ice turns into gas, and a glowing cloud forms around it. The Sun's energy pushes this material into a tail that can stretch for millions of miles.

The most famous comet is probably Halley's Comet. It returns to our part of the sky about every 75 or 76 years. The English astronomer Edmond Halley studied old records and correctly predicted that it would return in 1758. It was last seen from Earth in 1986, and it should appear again in 2061. I'll be pretty old by then, but I'm already planning to watch.

Many people think that summer happens because Earth moves closer to the Sun, but that isn't the reason. In fact, Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, which is winter in the United States. The real cause of the seasons is the tilt of Earth's axis.

Earth spins on an imaginary line that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole, and this line is tilted. As Earth travels around the Sun each year, the tilt stays pointed in the same direction. For part of the year, the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun. Sunlight strikes it more directly, and the days are longer, so it's summer there. Six months later, the Northern Hemisphere leans away, and the days grow short and cold. Meanwhile, countries like Australia and Argentina have their seasons at the opposite times of year.

Off the northeast coast of Australia lies the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef system on Earth. It stretches for about 1,400 miles and is made up of thousands of separate reefs and hundreds of islands. It is so large that astronauts can see it from space.

Although coral may look like colorful rocks or plants, it is actually made of tiny animals called polyps. Each polyp builds a hard skeleton around itself, and over thousands of years, these skeletons pile up to form reefs. The Great Barrier Reef is home to an amazing variety of life, including sea turtles, sharks, and more than a thousand kinds of fish. Scientists work hard to protect it, because coral can be harmed by pollution and by water that becomes too warm.

A glacier is a huge, slow-moving river of ice. Glaciers form in places where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, the snow piles up and gets pressed into thick ice. Eventually, the ice becomes so heavy that it begins to slide downhill, usually moving only a few inches or feet each day.

As glaciers creep along, they act like giant bulldozers. They scrape the land, pick up rocks, and carve deep valleys. Thousands of years ago, during the last ice age, glaciers covered much of Canada and the northern United States. When they melted, they left behind hills, boulders, and lakes. In fact, the Great Lakes were shaped in part by glaciers. Today, you can still visit glaciers in Alaska, Montana, and many other places.

When the tide went out on the rocky coast of Maine, my sister Grace and I grabbed our notebooks and a magnifying glass and headed for the tide pools. These small pools of seawater get trapped among the rocks when the ocean pulls back. At first, they looked empty, but when we knelt down and watched quietly, they came alive.

A green crab scuttled sideways under a ledge, and a periwinkle snail inched along the bottom. Grace spotted a purple sea star clinging to a rock, and I found a cluster of mussels with shiny blue shells. We were careful not to pull anything off the rocks, since many tide pool creatures can be hurt that way. Before the tide came back in, we filled our notebooks with drawings, and then we climbed back up to the beach to dry off.

It's easy to walk across the ground without thinking about it, but soil is one of the most important materials on Earth. Nearly all the food we eat depends on it. Soil forms very slowly, sometimes taking hundreds of years to build up just one inch.

The process begins when rock is broken into smaller pieces by wind, water, ice, and the roots of plants. This is called weathering. Over time, the tiny bits of rock mix with dead leaves, twigs, and other once-living things. Earthworms, insects, fungi, and bacteria break down this material into a dark, rich substance. It holds water and gives plants the nutrients they need to grow. Healthy soil also contains air spaces, which let roots breathe and water drain. Farmers and gardeners take care of their soil, because once it washes away, it's very hard to replace.

The Great Wall of China is not just one wall but a long series of walls, towers, and forts built over many centuries. Different Chinese rulers added to it, beginning more than two thousand years ago. Most of the sections that visitors see today were built during the Ming dynasty, which ruled from 1368 to 1644.

The wall was built to protect China's northern border. Soldiers stood guard in watchtowers, and they used smoke and fire signals to warn each other when trouble was coming. Building the wall was extremely hard work, and workers used stone, brick, and even packed earth. If you added together all of its branches, the total length would be more than 13,000 miles. Despite a popular myth, though, you can't really see the wall from the Moon.

In January 1848, a carpenter named James Marshall noticed something shiny in a stream at Sutter's Mill in California. It was gold. News of the discovery spread slowly at first, but by 1849, thousands of people were rushing west to strike it rich. These fortune seekers were nicknamed forty-niners, after the year they arrived.

The forty-niners came from all over the United States and from countries as far away as China, Chile, and Australia. They traveled by wagon, by ship, and on foot. Most of them panned for gold by swirling sand and water in a shallow metal dish. A few found great fortunes, but many found very little. Still, the Gold Rush changed California forever. San Francisco grew from a small town into a busy city, and California became a state in 1850.

The Statue of Liberty was a gift from the people of France to the United States. A French sculptor named Frederic Auguste Bartholdi designed it, and the engineer Gustave Eiffel planned the iron framework inside. Eiffel later became famous for building the Eiffel Tower in Paris.

The statue was built in France, then taken apart and shipped across the Atlantic Ocean in more than 200 crates. Meanwhile, Americans raised money to build the giant pedestal it would stand on. Many children donated their pennies to help. Finally, in 1886, the statue was put back together on an island in New York Harbor. Its copper skin was shiny brown at first, but over the years, it slowly turned the pale green color we see today.

Many people picture castles as grand palaces, but life inside a medieval castle was often cold, dark, and crowded. Castles were built mainly for protection. Their thick stone walls, narrow windows, and deep moats made them hard to attack. The great hall was the center of daily life, where the lord, his family, and their servants ate together at long wooden tables.

A castle was like a small village. Cooks prepared meals in the kitchen, blacksmiths made tools and horseshoes, and stable hands cared for the horses. Children of noble families learned to ride, read, and play music. Some boys trained to become knights, starting as pages around the age of seven. Without electricity or glass in many windows, people relied on candles, fireplaces, and heavy tapestries to keep their rooms warm and bright.

The narrow streets of the old city of Marrakesh, in Morocco, were already crowded when my family arrived at the market. Stalls overflowed with spices, dates, olives, and colorful woven rugs. The air smelled of mint and cinnamon, and merchants called out to shoppers in Arabic, French, and English.

My father bargained with a seller for a brass lantern, which is a normal part of shopping there. They went back and forth until they agreed on a fair price, and then they both smiled and shook hands. Later, we sat at a small cafe and drank sweet mint tea from tiny glasses. As the sun set, the main square filled with musicians, storytellers, and food stands. It was louder and busier than any place I'd ever been, and I loved every minute of it.

Canada is the second-largest country in the world by area, stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean and north to the Arctic. Even though it's so big, most Canadians live within a few hundred miles of the southern border with the United States. Its capital is Ottawa, and its largest city is Toronto.

Canada has two official languages, English and French. In the province of Quebec, most people speak French as their first language. The country is known for its vast forests, sparkling lakes, and rugged mountains. In fact, Canada has more lakes than any other country. The maple leaf on its red and white flag is a national symbol, and Canada produces most of the world's maple syrup. Hockey is hugely popular there, and many kids learn to skate almost as soon as they can walk.

When it's noon in New York, it's only nine in the morning in Los Angeles. That's because the world is divided into time zones. Earth makes one complete turn every 24 hours, so the Sun rises over different places at different times. If every city used the same clock, the Sun might be overhead at midnight in some places!

Before the 1880s, most towns in the United States set their clocks by the Sun, so nearby towns often had slightly different times. This caused confusion for railroads, which needed reliable schedules. In 1883, the railroads adopted standard time zones, and other countries soon created their own. Today, the world has about two dozen main time zones, roughly one for each hour of the day. The lower 48 states use four of them, which are Eastern, Central, Mountain, and Pacific.

Venice, Italy, is a city unlike any other. Instead of streets, it has canals, and instead of cars, people get around by boat or on foot. The city is built on more than one hundred small islands in a shallow lagoon, and they are linked by hundreds of bridges.

The largest waterway is the Grand Canal, which winds through the middle of the city in the shape of a backward S. Water buses carry passengers from stop to stop, and delivery boats bring groceries, packages, and even furniture. The most famous boats in Venice are gondolas, which are long, narrow, and painted black. A gondolier stands at the back and steers with a single oar. Because the city sits so low, high tides sometimes flood its squares, so the people of Venice have learned to live closely with the sea.

Last weekend, my grandmother taught me how to bake bread from scratch. We started by mixing warm water, sugar, and yeast in a large bowl. Within ten minutes, the mixture was foamy, which meant the yeast was alive and working. Then we added flour and salt, stirred everything together, and turned the sticky dough onto the counter.

Kneading was harder than I expected. Grandma showed me how to push the dough away with the heels of my hands, fold it over, and turn it. After about ten minutes, it felt smooth and stretchy. We left it in a warm spot to rise, and by the time we came back, it had doubled in size. Finally, we shaped it into a loaf and baked it. The whole house smelled wonderful, and the bread tasted even better than it smelled.

When my family moved from Texas to Oregon in August, I was nervous about starting sixth grade at a school where I didn't know anyone. On the first day, I stood in the doorway of the cafeteria holding my tray, wondering where to sit. Then a girl with curly hair waved at me from a table near the window.

Her name was Maya, and she had moved to town only a year earlier, so she knew exactly how I felt. She introduced me to her friends, showed me where the library was, and explained which teachers gave the most homework. By the end of the week, I had joined the art club and the robotics team. I still miss my old friends, and we talk on video every Sunday, but Oregon is starting to feel like home.

t: How to Write a Thank-You Note
x:
A handwritten thank-you note is a simple way to show someone that you appreciate them. It doesn't have to be long, but it should be sincere. Start with a greeting, such as "Dear Uncle Ray," and then thank the person for the specific gift or kind deed. Instead of writing "Thanks for the present," try something like "Thank you for the book about sharks."

Next, explain why it matters to you. You might say that you've already read three chapters or that you plan to use the gift on your next camping trip. Then add a friendly sentence about something else, such as an upcoming visit or a recent event in your life. Finally, sign your name with a warm closing, like "Love" or "Your friend." Mail it within a week or two, while the gift is still fresh in everyone's mind.

Every Friday, my family turns off the television and gathers around the kitchen table for game night. We take turns choosing the game, so everyone gets a fair chance to pick a favorite. My little brother always chooses a matching game, while my mom prefers word games, and my dad loves anything with dice.

Last week, it was my turn, and I picked a strategy game where players build roads and trade resources. It took almost two hours to finish, and the lead changed hands several times. In the end, my mom won by a single point, and we all groaned and then laughed. Afterward, we made popcorn and talked about our week. Game night isn't really about winning, though. It's about spending time together, and I think that's why it's my favorite night of the week.

The ancient Olympic Games were held in Greece for more than a thousand years, but they ended long ago. In the 1890s, a Frenchman named Pierre de Coubertin decided to bring them back. He believed that sports could build character and bring nations together in friendly competition.

The first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens, Greece, in 1896. About 240 athletes from 14 countries competed in events such as running, swimming, cycling, wrestling, and fencing. A Greek runner named Spyridon Louis won the marathon, and the crowd cheered so loudly that people said the stadium shook. Today, the Summer and Winter Olympics each take place every four years, and they feature thousands of athletes from more than 200 nations.

I got my first skateboard for my eleventh birthday, along with a helmet, knee pads, and elbow pads. My cousin Diego, who has been skating for years, offered to teach me. He said the first thing I needed to learn wasn't how to ride, but how to fall safely.

We practiced in an empty parking lot near the park. At first, I could barely balance, and I fell more times than I could count. Diego showed me how to bend my knees, keep my weight centered, and push off with my back foot. After a week, I could glide across the whole lot without stopping. Then I learned to turn by leaning my body to one side. I'm still not ready for the ramps, but I'm improving every day, and my bruises are healing too.

A baseball field is often called a diamond, because the four bases form a square that looks like a diamond from home plate. The bases are exactly 90 feet apart in the major leagues, a distance that has stayed the same for well over a century. Many fans believe this distance is nearly perfect, because a ground ball to the infield and a fast runner often reach first base at almost the same moment.

The pitcher stands on a small hill called the mound, which is 60 feet, 6 inches from home plate. A batter has less than half a second to decide whether to swing at a fast pitch. Baseball has been called America's pastime since the 1800s, and it's also very popular in countries such as Japan, the Dominican Republic, and Cuba.

A marathon is a footrace that covers 26.2 miles. According to a famous Greek legend, a messenger ran all the way from the town of Marathon to Athens to announce a victory. When the first modern Olympics were held in 1896, organizers created a long-distance race to honor that story.

At first, marathons were not all the same length. The distance of 26.2 miles was used at the 1908 Olympics in London, where the course ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium, and it became the official length in 1921. Today, cities such as Boston, New York, and Chicago host huge marathons each year. Runners train for months, slowly building up their distance. For most people, just crossing the finish line is a great achievement, whether they run, jog, or walk part of the way.

The Dutch artist Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in 1889, while he was living in the south of France. The painting shows a small village beneath a night sky filled with swirling clouds, glowing stars, and a bright crescent moon. A tall, dark cypress tree rises in the foreground like a flame.

Van Gogh used thick, bold brushstrokes, and you can almost feel the movement in the sky. Although he created around 900 paintings in about ten years, he sold very few during his lifetime. Today, he is one of the most famous painters in history, and The Starry Night hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York City. Every year, millions of visitors come to see his colorful works in museums around the world.

For months, our drama club rehearsed for the spring play, a comedy about a group of friends lost on a mysterious island. I played the captain, which meant I had more lines to memorize than I'd ever had before. I practiced at breakfast, on the bus, and while brushing my teeth, until my family could recite my lines too.

The night before the show, everything seemed to go wrong. A piece of scenery fell over, two actors forgot their entrances, and the lights flickered. Our director, Ms. Park, told us not to worry, since a rough dress rehearsal often means a great performance. She was right. On opening night, the audience laughed at all the jokes, and nobody missed a cue. When we took our bows, the applause was louder than I had ever imagined.

Have you ever wondered how a book travels from an author's imagination to a library shelf? The process usually takes a year or more. First, the author writes a manuscript, revising it many times. Then an editor reads it carefully and suggests ways to make the story clearer, stronger, or more exciting.

Once the words are finished, a designer chooses the fonts and lays out each page. If it's a picture book, an illustrator creates artwork that brings the characters to life. A copy editor checks for spelling and grammar mistakes, which is a lot like being a detective. Next, the pages are sent to a printer, where huge machines print, fold, and bind thousands of copies. Finally, the books are shipped to stores and libraries, where readers like you can discover them.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in 1756 in Salzburg, a city that is now part of Austria, and he showed amazing musical talent from a very young age. By the time he was five, he was already writing short pieces for the keyboard. His father, Leopold, was also a musician, and he took Wolfgang and his older sister, Nannerl, on long tours across Europe. The two children performed for kings, queens, and crowds of fascinated listeners.

As an adult, Mozart wrote more than 600 works, including symphonies, operas, and concertos. Some of his pieces are cheerful and playful, while others are calm and serious. He worked incredibly fast and often composed whole pieces in his head before writing them down. Even though he lived only thirty-five years, his music is still performed all over the world, and many people consider him one of the greatest composers who ever lived.

When someone uses a map on a phone to find a new restaurant, they're relying on a system called GPS, which stands for Global Positioning System. GPS depends on a group of about thirty satellites that circle Earth high above the ground. Each satellite constantly sends out signals that include the exact time.

A GPS receiver, such as the one inside a phone or car, picks up signals from several satellites at once. Because radio signals travel at a known speed, the receiver can figure out how far away each satellite is by measuring how long its signal took to arrive. By combining the distances from at least four satellites, it can pinpoint its location, often to within a few feet. The United States military first developed GPS, but today farmers, pilots, hikers, and drivers all depend on it every day.

The first bicycles looked very different from the ones we ride today. In 1817, a German inventor named Karl Drais built a wooden machine with two wheels, but it had no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along with their feet, a bit like a scooter.

Later inventors added pedals to the front wheel. To make these bikes go faster, builders made the front wheel larger and larger. The result was the high-wheeler, which had a giant front wheel and a tiny back one. It was fast, but it was also tall and wobbly, and falling off was common. In the 1880s, the safety bicycle appeared, with two wheels of equal size and a chain that turned the back wheel. Its design was so successful that most bikes still follow it today.

A microwave oven can heat a bowl of soup in a minute or two, much faster than a stove. It works by producing microwaves, which are invisible waves of energy similar to radio waves. A part called a magnetron creates the microwaves, and a small spinning fan spreads them around the inside of the oven. The metal walls reflect the waves, so they bounce back and forth through the food.

Microwaves make water particles in food spin and jiggle very quickly, and this motion creates heat. That is why foods with lots of water, like vegetables and soup, warm up quickly. The microwave oven was invented after an engineer named Percy Spencer noticed that a candy bar in his pocket had melted while he worked near radar equipment in the 1940s. Never put metal in a microwave, because it can cause sparks.

In the early 1800s, the fastest way to send a message across a country was by horse or by ship. That changed in 1844, when Samuel Morse sent a message over a telegraph wire from Washington to Baltimore. The telegraph used electricity to send pulses along a wire, and operators tapped out letters using Morse code, a system of dots and dashes.

Over the next century, inventors kept finding faster and easier ways to communicate. The telephone let people hear each other's voices, and radio carried sound through the air without wires. Later, computers and cell phones made it possible to send text messages, photos, and videos almost instantly. Today, you can share a message with a friend on the other side of the world in less than a second, something Morse could only have dreamed about.
